column1: The fifteen factors that decide the outcome — distilled from the full concept list. Fill the shaded columns together.

column3: How many clinicians you have, split by discipline and full-time vs. per-diem.
column4: The single biggest driver of how much a branch can deliver; everything else works within it.

column3: Each visit type is worth points — routine 1.0, SOC 2.5, recert 1.75, and so on.
column4: The common currency. The same headcount delivers very different capacity depending on the visit mix.

column3: The weekly points you plan toward, and the daily maximum a clinician should not exceed.
column4: Defines what “full” means. Plan to the target; the ceiling is the hard cap capacity can’t cross.

column3: The bookable points left each day after work already assigned.
column4: The live read leaders act on — green means take more, red means full.

column3: Open room limited to clinicians who can do assessments (SOC / eval).
column4: New starts can only be met by assessing capacity; this is what gates saying yes to a referral.

column3: On-demand capacity from per-diem and contract staff.
column4: The elastic cushion when full-time is exhausted; its real size depends on relationships, not just stated availability.

column3: Which zip codes each clinician actually covers.
column4: Capacity only counts if it can reach the patient; room in the wrong area is room you can’t use.

column3: New starts entering and patients discharging.
column4: A referral consumes capacity; a discharge reopens it. This is the demand that moves the whole board.

column3: The doctor-ordered number and cadence of visits per patient.
column4: Non-negotiable demand — it sets what must be scheduled and when, before any preference.

column3: Matching each visit to the right clinician by discipline, skill, area and current load.
column4: Good fit uses capacity efficiently; assigning by whoever’s free wastes it and strains clinicians.

column3: Loading more visits Monday–Tuesday instead of back-ending to Friday.
column4: A front-loaded week absorbs surprises; a back-loaded one turns any hiccup into missed visits.

column3: Keeping the same clinician with the same patient.
column4: Drives trust and outcomes, but competes with efficiency — a real trade-off leaders should set on purpose.

column3: Confirming visits with patients before the day.
column4: Cuts no-shows and wasted trips — the cheapest way to protect delivered visits.

column3: Covering a clinician’s day when they call out.
column4: One uncovered call-out cascades into a day of missed visits; how fast you backfill decides the damage.

column3: Whether each visit was completed, is in progress, or was missed — and whether a 30-day period has enough visits.
column4: Only completed visits become revenue, and too few in a period (LUPA) slashes payment. This is where money is won or lost.
